paragraphs: In reviewing the various works written on education, I cannot pass over Lord Chesterfield’s Letters in silence. Not that I intend to analyse his unmanly, immoral system, or even to gather any of the useful, shrewd remarks scattered through his frivolous correspondence — no, I only mean to reflect briefly on what they openly aim at: the art of gaining an early knowledge of the world. It is an art, I will venture to assert, that feeds in secret, like the worm in the bud, on the unfolding powers, and turns to poison the generous sap which ought to rise vigorously through the young frame, inspiring warm affections and great resolutions.

There is a reason for everything, says the wise man; and who would look for the fruits of autumn in the mild months of spring? But this is mere rhetoric, and I intend to reason with those worldly-wise instructors who, instead of training the judgment, implant prejudices, and harden a heart that gradual experience would merely have cooled. To my mind, an early acquaintance with human failings — or what is called knowledge of the world — is the surest way to shrink the heart and dampen that natural ardour of youth which gives rise not only to great talents but to great virtues. For the vain attempt to produce the fruit of experience before the sapling has put out its leaves only drains its strength and stops it from growing into a natural shape; just as the shape and strength of metals as they settle are damaged when the attraction of cohesion is disturbed. Tell me, you who have studied the human mind, is it not an odd way to fix principles, to show young people that principles are rarely stable? And how can habits fortify them, when example proves those habits to be deceptive? Why must the ardour of youth be damped like this, and the richness of imagination cut to the quick? Such dry caution may, admittedly, shield a character from worldly mishaps; but it will certainly rule out excellence in either virtue or knowledge. The stumbling-block that suspicion lays across every path will prevent any vigorous effort of genius or benevolence, and life will be robbed of its most alluring charm long before its calm evening, when man ought to withdraw into contemplation for comfort and support.

A young man who has been raised among friends at home, and encouraged to fill his mind with as much speculative knowledge as can be gained from reading and from the natural reflections prompted by youthful bursts of high spirits and by instinctive feelings, will go out into the world with warm and mistaken expectations. But this seems to be the course of nature; and in morals, as in matters of taste, we should heed her sacred signs, and not presume to lead where we ought humbly to follow.

In the world, few people act on principle; present feelings and early habits are the chief motives. But how deadened the former would be, and how the latter would turn into corroding iron fetters, if young people were shown the world exactly as it is, before any knowledge of mankind or of their own hearts, slowly gained through experience, had taught them forbearance! Their fellow creatures would then not be seen as frail beings like themselves, condemned to struggle with human failings, showing now the bright and now the dark side of their characters, and drawing from us love and disgust by turns; instead, they would be guarded against like beasts of prey, until every broad social feeling — in a word, humanity — was rooted out.

In life, by contrast, as we gradually discover the imperfections of our nature, we discover virtues as well; and when we mix with our fellow creatures and look at the same things they do, all sorts of circumstances bind us to them which are never considered by those who acquire a hasty, unnatural knowledge of the world. We watch a folly swell into a vice by almost imperceptible degrees, and we pity even as we blame; but if the hideous monster burst upon our sight all at once, fear and disgust, making us harsher than man ought to be, might lead us in blind zeal to usurp the role of the Almighty and condemn our fellow mortals to damnation — forgetting that we cannot read the heart, and that the seeds of the same vices lie hidden in our own.

I have already remarked that we expect more from instruction than instruction alone can achieve: for instead of preparing young people to meet the evils of life with dignity, and to gain wisdom and virtue by using their own faculties, we pile precept upon precept and demand blind obedience, when conviction ought to be brought home to their reason.

Suppose, for example, that a young person in the first ardour of friendship idolizes the beloved one — what harm can this mistaken, enthusiastic attachment do? Perhaps virtue must first appear in human form in order to impress young hearts; the ideal model, which a more mature and elevated mind looks up to and fashions for itself, would be beyond their sight. How can a man who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, love God? asked the wisest of men.

It is natural for the young to credit the first object of their affection with every good quality; and the emulation born of ignorance — or, more properly, of inexperience — draws out the mind that is capable of such an affection. Then, as time passes and perfection proves to be beyond mortal reach, virtue in the abstract comes to seem beautiful, and wisdom sublime. Admiration then yields to friendship in the true sense, because it is bound together by esteem; and the person walks alone, relying on heaven alone for that eager, emulous longing for perfection which always glows in a noble mind. But a man must gain this knowledge by exerting his own faculties; and this is surely the blessed fruit of disappointed hope! For He who delights in spreading happiness and showing mercy to the weak creatures who are learning to know him never planted a good inclination in us to be a tormenting will-o’-the-wisp.

We now let our trees spread with wild luxuriance, and do not expect to force the majestic marks of age upon youthful graces; we wait patiently until they have sent their roots deep and weathered many a storm. Is the mind, then, which advances towards perfection more slowly the greater its dignity, to be treated with less respect? To argue by analogy, everything around us is in a state of progress; and when an unwelcome knowledge of life brings something close to weariness of it, and the natural course of things shows us that all that is done under the sun is vanity, we are approaching the solemn close of the drama. The days of activity and hope are past, and the opportunities the first stage of existence has offered for rising in the scale of intelligence must soon be added up. A knowledge of the futility of life at this stage — or earlier, if experience has taught it — is very useful, because it is natural; but when a frail being is shown the follies and vices of man so that he may learn to guard prudently against the ordinary accidents of life by sacrificing his heart, it is surely not too harsh to call this the wisdom of this world, as opposed to the nobler fruit of piety and experience.

I will venture a paradox and state my opinion without reserve: if men were born only to complete a circle of life and death, it would be wise to take every step foresight could suggest to make life happy. Moderation in every pursuit would then be the highest wisdom; and the prudent pleasure-seeker might enjoy a fair measure of contentment, even though he neither cultivated his understanding nor kept his heart pure. If we were merely mortal, prudence would be true wisdom — or, more precisely, it would secure the greatest share of happiness over the whole of life; but any knowledge beyond the conveniences of life would be a curse.

Why should we ruin our health with close study? The exalted pleasure that intellectual pursuits give would hardly make up for the hours of lethargy that follow — especially if we must also count the doubts and disappointments that cloud our inquiries. Every inquiry ends in vanity and vexation: for the cause we most wanted to discover retreats before us like the horizon as we advance. The ignorant, on the other hand, are like children, who suppose that if they could only walk straight ahead they would eventually reach the place where the earth meets the clouds. Yet, disappointed as we are in our inquiries, the mind grows stronger through the exercise — strong enough, perhaps, to grasp the answers it may receive, at another stage of existence, to the anxious questions it asked when the understanding, on feeble wings, was fluttering around visible effects in the hope of plunging into the hidden cause.

The passions too, the winds of life, would be useless, if not harmful, if the matter that makes up our thinking being, once we had thought in vain, merely went to sustain plant life — to nourish a cabbage, or to blush in a rose. The appetites would then serve every earthly purpose, and yield a more moderate and lasting happiness. But the powers of the soul, which are of little use here and probably disturb our animal pleasures even while a sense of our own dignity makes us glory in them, prove that life is merely an education, a state of infancy, and that its only hopes worth cherishing must not be sacrificed. My conclusion, therefore, is that we ought to know precisely what we want education to achieve; for the immortality of the soul is contradicted by the conduct of many people who firmly profess to believe in it.

If your first concern is to secure comfort and prosperity on earth, leaving the future to take care of itself, you are acting prudently when you give your child an early insight into the weaknesses of his nature. You may not, admittedly, turn him into an Inkle; but do not imagine that someone who absorbed a low opinion of human nature very early will keep to more than the letter of the law, or will feel any need to rise much above the common standard. He may avoid gross vices, since honesty is the best policy; but he will never aim at great virtues. The example of writers and artists will illustrate this point.

I must therefore venture to doubt whether what has passed for an axiom in morals may not be a dogmatic assertion made by men who have coolly observed mankind through the medium of books; and I say, in flat contradiction to them, that regulating the passions is not always wisdom. On the contrary, it would appear that one reason why men have better judgment and more fortitude than women is undoubtedly this: that they give freer rein to the grand passions, and, by going astray more often, broaden their minds. If, then, by using their own reason, they settle on some stable principle, they probably owe it to the force of their passions — passions fed by FALSE views of life and allowed to leap the boundary that secures contentment. But if at the dawn of life we could soberly survey the scenes ahead as though in perspective, and see everything in its true colours, how could the passions ever grow strong enough to unfold the faculties?
